'''''Senna bicapsularis''''' is a species of the [[legume]] [[genus]] ''[[Senna (plant)|Senna]]'', native to northern [[South America]], from [[Panama]] south to [[Venezuela]] and [[Colombia]], and also the [[West Indies]].<ref>USDA (2007)</ref> Common names include '''rambling senna''' (formerly "cassia"), '''winter cassia''', '''Christmas bush''', '''money bush''', and '''yellow candlewood'''.<ref name=pier /> In [[Florida]], ''[[Senna pendula]]'' is usually cultivated as, and misapplied to, ''S. bicapsularis''.<ref>[https://gardeningsolutions.ifas.ufl.edu/mastergardener/newsletter/2018/more/cassia-confusion.html Christmas Cassia Causes Confusion] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130041842/https://gardeningsolutions.ifas.ufl.edu/mastergardener/newsletter/2018/more/cassia-confusion.html |date=2021-11-30 }} By Marc Frank, [[University of Florida]]</ref><ref>[https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/excluded.aspx?id=522 Senna bicapsularis]  Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florida, Tampa.</ref>

==Description==
It is a [[semi-evergreen]] [[shrub]] growing to 3.5 m tall with a low spreading crown that reproduces by seed. It can grow from 2 – 12 metres tall and it branches from near the base.

The [[leaf|leaves]] are 2.5–9 cm long, pinnate, with six to eight leaflets; the leaflets are 1.6–4.5 cm long and 1.1–2.3 cm broad. The yellow [[flower]]s are produced in masses with a few together on short [[raceme]]s and 12–16 mm long. The plant flowers from autumn to winter, attracting bees and butterflies.<ref name=pier/><ref>[https://garden.org/plants/view/71502/Christmas-Senna-Senna-bicapsularis/ Christmas Senna (Senna bicapsularis)] by The National Gardening Association.</ref>

''Senna bicapsularis'' is distinguished from ''[[Senna pendula]]'' by having 3 pairs of leaflets on each leaf and elongated [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s (flower stalks), while ''S. pendula'' has 4-7 pairs of leaflets on each leaf and a gland between each pair of leaflets, with shorter flower stalks. ''S. bicapsularis'' flowers from late fall to winter depending on climate, whilst ''S. pendula'' can flower from as early as late summer. ''Senna pendula'' can grow very easily from seed, while ''Senna bicapsularis'' has a tough seed coat that needs mechanical scarification to sprout with success.<ref>[https://www.floridagardener.com/cassia-bicapsularis/ CASSIA BICAPSULARIS] ''floridagardener.com''</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Nahuas]] of [[San Luis Potosi]] resort to this plant for the healing of the enchantment. For this reason, the patient is cleaned with seven of its leaves, passing them throughout the body. Likewise, as part of this treatment, while the healer prays, he perfumes the patient's body with a [[charcoal]], [[rosemary]] and [[copal]] incense and then cleanses it with an egg to remove the "bad air" that has taken possession of his body.<ref name="apmtm">{{cite web
|title=Palo hediondo
|url=http://www.medicinatradicionalmexicana.unam.mx/apmtm/termino.php?l=3&t=cassia-emarginata
|access-date=2026-09-11
|language=es
|work=Atlas de las Plantas de la Medicina Tradicional Mexicana
|publisher=Biblioteca Digital de la Medicina Tradicional Mexicana (BDMTM)
}}</ref>

The leaves are edible.{{Cite needed|date=September 2026}} The leaves are used to cure [[erysipelas]] in [[Morelos]], and as an [[antiseptic]] in [[Oaxaca]].<ref name="apmtm"/> The sap from emaciated leaves can be used externally, with salt, to heal [[rashes]], [[Ulcer (dermatology)|sore]]s, bites, stings, [[eczema]], [[scabies]], [[ringworm]] and [[candidiasis|thrush]].{{Cite needed|date=September 2026}} In the 20th century, Maximino Martínez points out the following uses: [[cathartic]] and to counteract the effects of [[arthropod]] stings, and, in Tierra Blanca, [[Veracruz]], a decoction of 60 g of fresh or dry leaves in 250 g of water as a remedy for [[whooping cough]].<ref name="martinez">{{cite book
|last=Martínez
|first=Maximino
|title=Las plantas medicinales de México
|edition=3rd
|year=1944
|publisher=Ediciones Botas
|location=México
|pages=356, 396
|language=es
|url=https://archive.org/details/lasplantasmedici00mart
|access-date=2026-09-11
}}</ref>

The seedpod flavour resembles [[tamarind]].<ref>{{cite book
|last=Morton
|first=Julia Frances
|title=Atlas of Medicinal Plants of Middle America: Bahamas to Yucatan
|publisher=Charles C. Thomas
|location=Springfield, Ill.
|year=1981
|pages=316–317
|isbn=9780398040369
|lccn=80-13503
}}</ref> The leaves can be cooked as a vegetable, which can be mixed with other leaves, [[bean]]s or [[pea]]s.{{Cite needed|date=September 2026}}

==Invasive species==
It is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] and [[invasive plant|invasive]] in several coastal areas in the tropics, including [[Tanzania]], [[Kenya]], the [[Galápagos Islands]] and [[New Caledonia]], where it is found in roadsides and disturbed areas, wooded grasslands, [[fallow]] land and [[riparian]] zones.<ref name=pier>PIER (2006)</ref><ref>Henderson, L. (2001).  Alien weeds and invasive plants. A complete guide to declared weeds and invaders in South Africa.  Plant Protection Research Institute Handbook No. 12, 300pp. PPR, ARC South Africa.</ref>

===Chemistry===
The leaves and stems contain chaksinelike [[alkaloid]]s. The seeds contain [[galactomannan]]. The presence in the plant of cassin, 2,6-[[dialkyl]]-3-hydroxypyridine and socassidine has also been reported.

==Synonyms==
[[File:Fragmenta botanica, figuris coloratis illustrata (T. 58) BHL287687.jpg|thumb|Botanical illustration]]
''Senna bicapsularis'' has been described under a wide variety of names that are today considered its [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]]s. Some of these were also applied to related plants in error. This phenomenon has happened with other [[taxa]], which were mis-applied to this plant:<ref>ILDIS (2005)</ref>
* ''Adipera bicapsularis'' <small>(L.) Britton & Wilson</small>
* ''Adipera spiciflora'' <small>Pittier</small>
* ''Cassia berterii'' <small>Colla</small>
* ''Cassia bicapsularis'' <small>L.</small>
:''Cassia bicapsularis'' <small>''sensu'' Bojer</small> is erroneous for ''[[Senna pendula]]''.
:''Cassia bicapsularis'' of other authors is erroneous for ''Senna pendula'' var. ''glabrata''
* ''Cassia bicapsularis'' <small>L.</small> var. ''aristata'' <small>DC.</small>
:''Cassia aristata'' <small>Benth.</small> is a synonym of ''[[Chamaecrista aristata]]''
* ''Cassia bicapsularis'' <small>L.</small> var. ''quadrijuga'' <small>DC.</small>
* ''Cassia collae'' <small>G.Don</small>
* ''Cassia emarginata'' <small>L.</small>
:''Cassia emarginata'' <small>Clos</small> is a synonym of ''[[Senna candolleana]]''
:''Cassia emarginata'' <small>Mill.</small> is a synonym of ''[[Chamaecrista pilosa]]''
* ''Cassia inflata'' <small>Spreng.</small>
* ''Cassia laevigata'' <small>''sensu'' Prain</small>
:''Cassia laevigata'' <small>Willd.</small> is a synonym of ''[[Senna septemtrionalis]]''
:''Cassia laevigata'' of other authors  is erroneous for ''[[Senna occidentalis]]''
* ''Cassia limensis'' <small>Lam.</small>
* ''Cassia sennoides'' <small>Jacq.</small>
* ''Cassia spiciflora'' <small>(Pittier) Pittier</small>
* ''Cathartocarpus bicapsularis'' <small>(L.) Ham.</small>
* ''Chamaefistula inflata'' <small>G.Don</small>
* ''Isandrina arborescens'' <small>Raf.</small>
* ''Isandrina emarginata'' <small>(L.) Britton & Rose</small>
